input:
In this worked example, the aim is to compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and to determine the fraction of the reactant that remains after 60 min. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) through the relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after a time t (min) is given by exp(-k t). It is worth emphasising that the half-life depends on the rate constant alone; the amount of material present at the start has no bearing on it, and the same fraction disappears in each successive half-life for as long as the reaction remains first order in character.

The measured rate constant is k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. Substituting the measured value into the half-life relation gives the half-life as 15.1 min. Turning to the fraction remaining after 60 min, the exponent is -(0.046 x 60) = -2.76, so that exp(-2.76) = 0.06: the great majority of the reactant has been consumed, as one would expect after an interval amounting to four half-lives in round terms, since repeated halving over such a span leaves only a small residue behind. It should be noted, however, that these relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law altogether, and the figures arrived at here do not carry over to such a case.
